title: The case for games on personal AI agents (essay/longread)
author: agentaya-ltd
selftext:
The current generation of consumer AI agents is being sold mostly as a personal assistant, a ‘worker’ to help its human owner.

Instinct opened its private beta in August 2026 and Meta launched their Muse agent in September, and nearly all the use cases that get written about are tasks: chasing a refund, cancelling an unused subscription, finding a cheaper broadband deal, booking a restaurant. Forbes reported in September that tasks related to saving or recovering money looked like the most popular uses so far. Which makes sense as a starting point, because these tasks are easy to explain and the value is easy to see, even for people who are less tech- or AI savvy.

The problem with tasks like these is that people run out of them. Most people switch broadband once a year at most, and a cancelled subscription stays cancelled. Chat assistants already show where usage drifts when people are left to themselves: OpenAI's own study of ChatGPT found that non-work related messages grew from 53% to more than 70% of consumer use in about a year. People clearly want AI in the rest of their lives, and so far, hardly anyone has given them a reason to play with it.

That is likely to change. Every consumer computing platform of the last 40 years has ended up full of games, usually sooner than its makers expected. Games gave people a reason to come back every day, brought in people who would not otherwise have shown up, and in several cases also paid a large chunk of the bills.

There are good reasons to expect the same on agent platforms.

**Games follow new platforms**

It started with the PC. Microsoft shipped Solitaire with Windows 3.0 in 1990 and Minesweeper with Windows 3.1 in 1992. The fascinating story behind these games, is that they were there to teach people used to command lines how to drag, drop and right-click etc: in 1994 Microsoft's product manager for entertainment told the Washington Post that Solitaire was meant to make Windows less intimidating and teach people the mouse along the way. Within a few years the complaint was that office workers were playing too much of it.

Facebook is mabye the clearest example. When it opened to outside developers in 2007 it had no plans to become a games platform, yet by the end of 2010 about half of its monthly users were playing games. Zynga's 2011 IPO filing showed 60 million people playing its games every day, and a few months later Facebook's own filing revealed that Zynga alone accounted for 12% of its 2011 revenue, with social games producing almost all of its payments revenue. Games were the first thing people paid for on Facebook, and the first sign that other companies could build a real business there, on top of this platform.

Mobile repeated the pattern at a much bigger scale. As late as 2019, games were about a third of downloads on the App Store and Google Play but accounted for 75% of consumer spending. That share has fallen since, and Sensor Tower expected games to drop below half of App Store spending by 2026 as subscriptions to other apps grew. But games carried much of the platform's economics in its early years.

WeChat may be the closest precedent, because it already looks like what agent platforms probably want to become: one app that sits on top of everything else, with other services running inside it. Tencent added mini games at the end of 2017, and the first one, a simple jumping game called Jump Jump, reached 100 million daily players within weeks. More than half of the people playing mini games at the time did not play regular mobile games at all. WeChat mini games now have more than 500 million monthly players.

Not every platform shift worked out for games of course. Play-to-earn crypto games, and later the tap-to-earn games on Telegram, drew huge numbers that disappeared just as quickly. Hamster Kombat claimed 300 million players in mid-2024 and was down to 41 million by November, shortly after its token launched.

People who come to earn leave when the money stops, while people who come to play tend to keep playing.

**Why platforms should embrace games**

The main reason is frequency of use. Most of what agents do well happens a few times a year: a holiday to book, a contract to renew, a refund to chase. These tasks are why people sign up, but they do not build a habit, and agents are subscription products. Muse, for example, is free to start and then $20 or $100 a month, and a subscription people only use a few times a year is one they will eventually cancel. Games are the most reliable daily habit consumer software has found.

Some of the best evidence comes from companies that are not in the games business. LinkedIn launched three small daily puzzles in 2024 and now has eight. It says 86% of players come back the next day and 82% are still playing a week later, and that around 40% of new players find the games through results their connections share. LinkedIn has also said that people who come back daily to play go on to read more of everything else, sponsored posts included. If games work on a professional network, it is hard to think of a platform where they would not.

The New York Times tells a similar story. Its puzzles were played more than 11 billion times in 2025, and its head of games has said that subscribers who use both news and games each week have the best retention of any group the company has measured. People subscribe for the journalism and the puzzles help keep them paying. Agent platforms could use games in the same way, to keep people around between the occasions when they need a flight changed or a bill disputed.

The second reason is audience. The early users of agents that hold your passwords and payment details are mostly people comfortable with technology and with risk. Games reach a much wider and older group. AARP research from 2026 found that about 60 million Americans over 50 play video games, mostly puzzle, card and word games on their phones, with women more likely than men to play daily. The same study found that 79% usually play alone, and that while 40% say games are part of their daily routine, only 10% think of themselves as gamers. That is a very large group of people who play every day, mostly on their own, and an agent that can deal a hand of rummy or set a crossword at the right level is an easy way in for exactly the people least likely to hand over their bank login. WeChat saw the same effect when most of its mini game players turned out to be people who did not play other mobile games.

Games are also a low-risk way to learn a new kind of interface, which is what Solitaire was doing in 1990. Most people do not yet know what to ask an agent or how far to trust it. A game shows how it follows instructions, what it remembers and how it deals with mistakes, with nothing at stake if it gets something wrong.

Finally, games bring business models with them. On Facebook and on phones they were the first category where people paid for things inside someone else's platform, and agent platforms are still working out how to make money beyond subscriptions and usage limits.

**Why game developers/creators should care**

For developers, the most useful thing a new platform offers, is ‘space’ – call it a new dawn, a new opportunity. The early years of Facebook and the App Store were great times for small studios because there was an audience and little competition. Both filled up quickly, and today success on mobile depends heavily on how much you can spend acquiring players. Agent platforms are still close to empty, so whoever works out what a good game on an agent looks like will be building for an audience with very little else to play.

There is no shortage of people who could build those games. By one estimate, the games industry cut around 8,500 jobs in 2022, 10,500 in 2023, more than 15,600 in 2024 and about 9,000 in 2025, and many of those people now work alone or in small teams.

The pool of people who can make a game at all has grown as well. In February 2025 Pieter Levels, who had never made a game before, built a browser flight simulator with an AI coding tool in a few hours and reported $1 million in annualised revenue 17 days later. Platforms built around this kind of creation are growing too. Astrocade, which turns text prompts into games, reported 10 million monthly players by October 2026, and its largest group of users is women aged 20 to 40, which is not the usual picture of a game developer. Roblox, the most mature version of this model, paid creators more than $1 billion in the year to June 2025, although the median creator in its payout programme earned $1,440 and most of the money went to a small number of hits.

Agents also give developers some things other platforms cannot. The first is the agent itself. A game can assume that every player has a capable opponent, partner, narrator or referee available at no extra cost, which makes room for formats that were hard to build before: bluffing and negotiation games, murder mysteries where the suspects answer questions, quizzes with a host who reacts to your answers. Research has shown this is very much possible: in 2022 Meta's Cicero played the negotiation game Diplomacy against people online and scored more than twice the human average, by talking, persuading and making deals with the other players.

The second is real, deep personalisation. An agent knows what its owner likes, how hard they want things to be and how much time they usually have, and a game that can ask can adjust to each player without the developer building all of that from scratch. The third is that the person making the game no longer needs to be a developer. People already ask chatbots for quizzes and word games for a family dinner or a long car journey, and agents can turn those into something that lasts, whether it is played by one person, a group of friends or anyone who finds it. Most of those games will only ever matter to a few people, which is how house rules and family card games have always worked.

**What players get**

Most multiplayer games share one problem, which is other people. The ADL's survey of US online gamers found that 76% of adults and three quarters of 10 to 17 year olds experienced harassment in online games in 2023. Below that level there are the ordinary frustrations: opponents who quit when they are losing, friends who have to stop after two rounds, someone leaving you waiting mid-move because their UberEats delivery has arrived... An agent is available at any hour, does not sulk, shout or leave early, and can maybe play a little weaker while you learn or a little stronger when you want a challenge.

People also seem to enjoy playing against software with some personality. In January 2023, the largest online chess platform released a set of cat-themed bots, including Mittens, a very strong engine with a cheerful and slightly menacing chat persona. Players played 120 million games against the cat bots that month, and the site had its busiest month up to that point. Mittens had a handful of scripted lines, whereas an agent can hold a real conversation and remember the last game you played.

An agent can also take on roles other than opponent. It can partner you against a friend and their agent, host a quiz that includes your family's in-jokes, narrate a murder mystery, make up the numbers when a card game needs four and you have three, or coach you through why you lost. It can organise the game too, finding a time that works for six friends, sending the invites and booking a table, which is the kind of task agents are already being built for. Bots and tutorials have covered some of these roles in video games for years, but now one agent can cover all of them, across any game that supports it, for a player it already knows.

This matters for people who mostly play alone, which according to AARP is most older players. It also points to something parents might want. Most consumer agents are currently for adults only, but a parent's agent that can set up a game for a young child, keep strangers out, keep the conversation appropriate and end play at bedtime would be a more natural idea than yet another set of parental controls hidden in a settings menu.

Then there are the games nobody has made yet. Facebook produced the asynchronous farming game, the iPhone the one-thumb endless runner, and the web the daily shareable puzzle. Agents will probably produce formats of their own, perhaps games played through an agent rather than directly, games that run in the background over several days, or games that are partly negotiations between agents.

**Some concerns and objections**

**People do not use AI assistants for games.** This is true for now, and it is the strongest objection. Games are a tiny share of ChatGPT use, and there is no public evidence yet of a hit game on an agent platform. But that figure measures what people do with a text box that was never designed for play, and nobody farmed on Facebook in 2007 or expected to solve puzzles on LinkedIn either.

**It costs too much to run.** A game played through a large model costs more per turn than a game of Candy Crush. Most of a game can run as normal code, though, with the model only used where judgement or conversation is needed, and the price of a given level of AI capability has been falling by about ten times a year.

**Platforms will not want to look frivolous.** Agent companies are asking people to trust them with passwords and payment details, and a games section might seem to undercut that. Microsoft had the same worry about Solitaire in offices, and LinkedIn, about as serious as consumer platforms get, decided that puzzles made it more useful. The games can also come from third parties, as they did on Facebook and WeChat.

**Building on someone else's platform is risky.** That is fair. Platforms change their rules, copy what works and take a bigger cut once they can, and agents add a new version of the risk because websites can block them: Amazon now shows Muse a warning calling it an unauthorised agent. Developers will want games that work across many agents, and platforms that want games will need to set clear rules early. The early App Store and Roblox both suggest that the platforms that treat developers well end up with the best games.

**Games built for engagement can cause harm.** This is a real concern, and agents raise the stakes because they know a lot about the player and can be very persuasive. A game played with an agent should behave like a good opponent at a board game: open about how it works, happy to stop, and not designed to keep a lonely person playing at 2am. The platforms that sort this out before regulators do will be the ones parents and older players trust.

**Agents will be used to cheat.** If an agent can play chess, it can play chess on your behalf against someone else. Games that mix people and agents need to be clear about who is actually playing, which favours formats where the agent's role is out in the open.

**This is just Web3 again.** Play-to-earn failed because people came for the money. The case for games on agents rests on the reasons people have always played, which is what worked on PCs, Facebook, phones and WeChat.

**Early days**

Games are unlikely to be the main reason people use personal agents, in the same way they were never the main reason people joined Facebook or bought a smartphone. What they did on those platforms was give people a reason to come back on days when they had nothing else to do there, bring in new kinds of users, teach newcomers how things worked and, in the early years, bring in a lot of the money. Agent platforms have the same gaps today: a narrow audience, infrequent use and business models that are still being worked out.

The platforms most likely to benefit will be the ones that make it easy and safe for others to build games, set clear rules on what games can do with the agent and the player's data, and then let developers get on with it. It is still early, and this is a forecast rather than a finding, but four decades of consumer platforms all point in the same direction…
